title: Canary cells: deliberately weakened sentinels set per-subarray refresh
idea: Forced connection to the coal-mine canary: each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with ~60% of normal Cs (truncated pillar or partial plate), written to '1' and sensed every window; their first failures set that subarray's refresh interval through a tiny on-die state machine instead of a global worst-case 32/64 ms.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: typical subarrays run 4-8x longer intervals while the weakened canaries bound tail risk; ~60-75% less refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Sourdough starter: OS-donated cold pages become living spare rows
idea: Like a starter fed from each batch, an OS balloon driver donates 0.5-1% of free pages to the memory controller, which remaps rows showing correctable-error growth or hammer susceptibility into them; pages are handed back under memory pressure and the starter is re-fed from the next free batch.
why: Lets fabs ship dies with 5-10x more weak rows than the fused-spare budget allows; raises sellable bits per wafer ~3-8% and extends field life with zero capex.

title: Zipper pairing: interlock weak and strong columns across chips per codeword
idea: Zipper teeth alternate: at module test each chip's retention-weak column groups are profiled and a per-DIMM permutation table in the RCD/buffer reroutes column bits so every ECC codeword pairs one chip's weak column only with other chips' strong columns, guaranteeing at most one weak bit per codeword.
why: A SEC code that dies at two weak bits now tolerates dies with ~10x the weak-cell density; marginal dies get binned into ECC DIMMs, ~5% more sellable bits.

title: Ant pheromone: analog decaying charge counters track row activations
idea: Each ACT deposits a fixed charge packet on a tiny per-row 'pheromone' capacitor beside the wordline driver; it leaks with a designed time constant near tREFW and a comparator fires a neighbor refresh at threshold, so the trail's evaporation is the sliding window for free.
why: Fact 9 (flips at ~1k ACTs): exact per-row tracking for ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row, <0.3% area versus 1-3% for SRAM/CAM counters.

title: Library late fees: refresh debt budgeted against ECC correction margin
idea: Rows accrue a 'fine' equal to predicted bit-error probability (temperature, elapsed time, profiled retention class); the controller refreshes a row only when expected errors in its codewords approach a set fraction of the code's correction capacity, so healthy rows run overdue for seconds.
why: Fact 3: converts idle ECC slack into skipped refreshes, ~50-80% refresh reduction at <=1e-15 uncorrectable rate.

title: Tetris placement: compressed payload shifted so slack lands on weak bits
idea: Lines are compressed (BDI/FPC); the controller keeps a per-row weak-bit mask and rotates/offsets the compressed payload inside the 64 B line so known-weak or stuck positions fall into padding, recorded by a 3-6 bit shift field - PCM stuck-at masking ported to DRAM retention tails.
why: ~40% of lines become immune to known weak cells with no extra parity, permitting longer refresh or acceptance of cheaper, leakier dies.

title: Origami fold: subarray product code repairs whole-row hammer bursts
idea: Fold each subarray into a 2D grid: per-line ECC along rows plus one XOR parity row per 64 rows, kept current on writes via in-DRAM bitwise row operations or buffer-die read-modify-write, so a row riddled with hammer flips is rebuilt from the column parity as an erasure.
why: Fact 9: turns catastrophic multi-bit row-hammer and whole-row failures into correctable erasures at ~1.6% capacity, allowing relaxed hammer thresholds and fewer mitigation refreshes.

title: Fire sprinkler: margin-sniffing sense amps trigger local auto-repair
idea: A second, offset-biased comparator per sense-amp group flags any activate whose bitline differential is under ~40 mV; flagged rows are immediately re-restored and logged on-die, and repeat offenders are remapped through soft PPR with no host involvement - a sprinkler that fires only where the heat is.
why: Catches weakening cells (retention, VRT, hammer) before they flip, making every read a free audit; supports ~2x longer refresh and smaller Cs margins.

title: Piano tuner: in-field sense-amp offset auto-zeroing during refresh idle
idea: Like periodic retuning, each sense amp samples its own offset against a shorted dummy bitline pair in spare refresh slots and stores a correction on a small trim capacitor or 3-bit DAC, cancelling both mismatch and aging drift.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: cutting effective SA offset ~20-30 mV lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3.5 fF (or AR from ~70:1 to ~50:1) at the same error rate.

title: Insurance pool: rack-level erasure coding across CXL memory devices
idea: As insurers pool risk, a CXL switch stripes each 4 KB page across 10+2 memory devices with Reed-Solomon parity computed in the switch, so individual devices can drop on-die ECC, chipkill and most spare rows and may even lose whole banks.
why: Removes ~12% ECC plus spare area per device and admits lower-grade dies; 20% pooled parity covers device-level failures across the rack.

title: Recycling sorter: sell retention-binned 'harvest grade' DRAM with mandated controller ECC
idea: Dies failing JEDEC 64 ms retention but passing at 16 ms or under stronger ECC are graded into a new SKU for AI KV-cache and cold-tier buyers whose controllers run 4x refresh or LDPC, with a standard grade label and warranty model so the parts are bankable.
why: Recovers ~5-15% of wafer output now scrapped or downgraded; pure supply gain without new fabs, helium or EUV.

title: Cicada primes: prime-stride randomized TRR sampling defeats synchronized hammering
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime cycles to dodge predator sync; TRR samplers use reseeded pseudo-random prime-length windows (e.g. 61/67/71 ACTs) so many-sided patterns that phase-lock to fixed sampling intervals cannot align with the blind spots.
why: Fact 9: restores in-DRAM TRR effectiveness at ~zero area, deferring costly per-row counters by a node or two.

title: Spider web: dual-end wordline drive tolerates mid-line opens
idea: Each wordline segment is driven from both ends, with a weak keeper at the far end, so a single open (void, CMP break) still leaves both halves driven - a web that holds after one strand snaps; only shorts consume spare rows.
why: Opens are a large share of row repairs; ~30-50% fewer spare rows needed, returning array area and raising yield.

title: Bicycle chain: spatially coupled LDPC links codewords along a row
idea: Each 64 B line's parity also covers slices of its neighbors like chain links, forming a spatially coupled LDPC across a 1 KB page that a sliding-window decoder in the base/buffer die resolves while the page is open.
why: Near-capacity correction at ~6% overhead versus 12.5%, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4: enough to use much smaller Cs or far longer refresh.

title: Immune memory: VRT suspects remembered forever via controller Bloom filter
idea: Variable-retention-time cells toggle good/bad and evade one-shot profiling; any address that ever yields a correctable error enters a counting Bloom filter (the 'memory T-cells'), and rows holding suspects get permanent 2x refresh or a stronger code.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: neutralizes VRT, the main reason profile-guided refresh is distrusted, unlocking safe 4x+ refresh relaxation.

title: Kintsugi spares: repair rows built stronger, doubling as high-retention zone
idea: As gold-filled cracks become the strongest part, spare rows are built at relaxed pitch with ~1.5x Cs; repaired rows become the sturdiest, and unused spares are exposed as a long-retention region for page tables and ECC metadata refreshed 8x less often.
why: Turns the ~2-5% spare area from dead silicon into useful, ultra-reliable capacity and protects critical metadata.

title: Hourglass: lifetime-tagged tensors stored in refresh-free rows
idea: The compiler/runtime tags tensors whose lifetime is shorter than the profiled retention floor (activations, gradients alive <20 ms); the controller places them in banks with refresh suspended, and timed-out data is treated as expired rather than corrupted - the sand runs out only after the data is dead.
why: Fact 3: in training 30-60% of DRAM traffic is short-lived; those rows stop paying refresh energy and bandwidth.

title: Bamboo septum: buried electron-sink implant between adjacent storage nodes
idea: Like bamboo's node walls that stop splits, a narrow grounded n+ sink implanted in the isolation between a buried wordline and the neighbor storage node collects electrons injected when the aggressor toggles, before they reach the victim.
why: Fact 9: attacks the charge-migration hammer mechanism directly; could raise flip thresholds from ~1k toward ~10k ACTs at <3% cell area.

title: Beehive geometry: staggered wordlines so no victim has one dominant aggressor
idea: Cells sit on a hexagonal lattice where each storage node's three nearest wordlines are distinct and roughly equidistant, so hammering any single row delivers about a third of today's coupling and a double-sided attack needs three coordinated rows.
why: Fact 9: ~2-3x higher effective hammer threshold from geometry alone, buying time for cheap mitigations.

title: Jazz wrong notes: bit-plane retention tiers for AI weights and KV-cache
idea: In jazz a wrong note resolves into the next; BF16/FP8 tensors are stored transposed by bit-plane, with sign/exponent/high-mantissa planes in normally refreshed rows and low-mantissa planes in rows with 8-16x longer refresh and no ECC, where flips dissolve into model noise.
why: Fact 3: roughly half of AI bits tolerate 1e-4 BER, cutting refresh power and ECC overhead on half the capacity.

title: Tattoo map: weak-row map inked into on-die OTP, standardized in JEDEC
idea: The fab's retention and hammer test map is permanently burned into on-die antifuse OTP in a standard JEDEC 'weak map' register format, so any controller can read it and apply targeted refresh, ECC placement or remapping.
why: Fabs over-design because controllers are blind; a standard map lets them ship lower-Cs, higher-variability dies for ~10% density/yield gain.

title: Lighthouse rotation: a vacated rotating subarray enables continuous online stress testing
idea: One subarray per bank is always empty and the vacancy sweeps around the bank like a lighthouse beam (data moved by in-DRAM row copy); while empty, it is stress-tested at full speed for retention, hammer and VRT and the weak map is updated with no downtime.
why: Aging and VRT invalidate fab profiles; continuous safe profiling enables aggressive 4x profile-guided refresh and early retirement for ~1.5% capacity.

title: Thrift store: refurbished hyperscaler DIMMs rehomed behind CXL ECC expanders
idea: Retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs are field-tested, binned and mounted on CXL expander cards whose controllers add symbol-level ECC, sparing and patrol scrub, giving them a second 3-5 year life as memory-tier capacity.
why: Adds GB supply with zero fab capex and zero new helium or quartz; the secondhand pool is hundreds of petabytes.

title: Desert cactus: Ga2O3 access transistors keep cells hydrated at 125 C
idea: The cactus's thick skin hoards water: a 4.8 eV bandgap Ga2O3 channel deposited by mist-CVD/ALD in BEOL forms the vertical access transistor over silicon-formed capacitors, where intrinsic generation at 125 C is negligible and off-current can stay <1e-20 A for 10 years.
why: Fact 3 at the 125 C/10-year constraint: retention stays at seconds instead of ~4-8 ms for silicon at 125 C, erasing the 8x hot-refresh penalty; goes beyond IGZO with a wider gap.

title: Thermostat wordline: off-voltage tracks temperature to the leakage minimum
idea: At each temperature the access transistor's total leakage (subthreshold vs GIDL) has a minimum at a specific negative wordline voltage; an on-die sensor and table steer VNWL from about -0.2 V at 25 C to about -0.5 V at 125 C, re-trimmed yearly to follow aging.
why: Fact 3 under 125 C for 10 years: ~2-4x lower hot leakage than a fixed VNWL, halving hot refresh while avoiding the constant GIDL field that accelerates oxide wear.

title: Camera pixel: pinned storage-node junction suppresses 125 C generation leakage
idea: Automotive image sensors beat 125 C dark current with a p+ surface pinning layer; the same shallow pinning implant over the storage-node junction surface plus an STI-sidewall passivation liner removes surface-state generation, the dominant hot leakage term.
why: Sensors cut dark current ~10x this way; the cell leakage tail at 125 C could fall 3-10x, allowing normal 64 ms refresh at 125 C through 10 years.

title: One-way street: Z-channel asymmetric codes for unidirectional hot retention errors
idea: At 125 C nearly all errors are charged-to-discharged; mapping every cell to logical polarity (true/anti cells) makes the channel a one-way Z-channel, and asymmetric codes correct t unidirectional errors with ~30-40% fewer parity bits than symmetric BCH.
why: Same ~6% overhead corrects ~2x more hot retention errors, allowing ~2x longer refresh at 125 C over the 10-year life.

title: Hotel keycard: polarity encoding minimizes charged cells; empty rows skip refresh
idea: Like lights cutting off when the keycard leaves, each line stores a polarity bit chosen to minimize physically charged cells, and rows whose cells are all discharged (zeroed or free pages) set a per-row flag that skips refresh entirely.
why: Only charged cells leak: at 125 C halving the charged population and exempting empty rows (often 20-40% of memory) slashes hot refresh energy and exposure over 10 years.

title: Mattress flipping: periodic true/complement inversion balances 10-year aging stress
idea: As mattresses are flipped to even wear, every few hours the controller rewrites each row inverted with a per-row polarity flag, so sense-amp pairs and capacitor dielectrics see balanced bias and BTI offset drift and polarity-dependent dielectric imprint stay symmetric at 125 C.
why: Ten years at 125 C can shift SA offset ~20-40 mV; balancing roughly halves drift, saving ~15% Cs margin or end-of-life refresh headroom.

title: Chameleon cells: auto-switch 1T1C to twin-cell 2T2C above 105 C
idea: Wordline decoders support a paired mode where two adjacent rows store complementary data on one sense amp (differential twin cell); above 105 C the OS shrinks the hot region and the controller migrates its pages into paired mode, doubling signal margin.
why: Twin cells tolerate ~4-10x more leakage, so parts survive 125 C for 10 years while cooler deployments keep full 1T1C density - no cell designed for worst case.

title: Food freshness label: on-die Arrhenius dose integrator for life-aware derating
idea: Like time-temperature indicator labels on food, a tiny on-die structure (a floating node leaking through thermally activated oxide, cross-checked by a BTI ring oscillator) integrates cumulative thermal stress; firmware reads the 'age' and tightens refresh, VNWL and ECC mode as the dose nears 10 years at 125 C equivalent.
why: Parts in milder missions run ~2x relaxed refresh while hot ones are protected to the 125 C/10-year budget; cuts lifetime guard-band ~20-30%.

title: Pressure cooker: high-pressure deuterium anneal plus nitride reservoir hardens interfaces
idea: Cook wafers in ~20 atm D2 at ~400 C so access-transistor and storage-node interfaces are passivated with Si-D (several times more resistant to depassivation than Si-H), capped by a deuterium-rich SiN reservoir that re-passivates bonds broken during 10 years at 125 C.
why: Interface-trap growth drives retention-tail drift at high temperature; ~3-10x slower drift keeps refresh constant over life.

title: Retread tires: consumer dies plus ECC chiplet qualified to AEC-Q100 Grade 1
idea: Retreading puts new tread on a sound carcass: commodity dies that fail 125 C retention are co-packaged with a small logic chiplet (refresh manager, asymmetric ECC, weak-row remap, thermal dose tracking) so the package meets Grade 1 (-40 to 125 C, 10-year mission).
why: Automotive/industrial DRAM is a constrained premium niche; reclassifying commodity output raises usable supply and suits U.S. OSAT packaging.

title: Penguin huddle: rotate long-lived data through stack thermal zones
idea: Penguins rotate between the cold edge and warm center; in a 3D stack or multi-die module the controller tracks per-die temperature and periodically migrates long-lived pages so no data and no die sits in the hottest 125 C zone continuously.
why: Hotspot dies age and leak fastest; equalizing dose cuts worst-case 10-year Arrhenius exposure ~2x and lets cooler dies run lower refresh.

title: Sauna recovery: on-die micro-heaters anneal traps after data evacuation
idea: Blocks of the array embed TiN resistive heaters; monthly, a block is evacuated by row copy, heated to ~250 C for seconds to recover BTI and anneal interface traps, then returned to service.
why: Repeatedly resets the aging clock during 10 years at 125 C, holding leakage tail and SA offset near time-zero and removing ~20-30% end-of-life retention margin.

title: Bonsai pruning: planned capacity shrink retires weakest rows yearly
idea: Instead of every cell meeting 10 years at 125 C at fab, the module ships with a declared pruning curve and asks the OS (CXL/ACPI hot-remove) to offline its weakest ~0.5% of rows per year based on in-field aging data, under a contractual capacity schedule.
why: Admits cheaper, less over-designed dies with ~5% yield/density gain while still guaranteeing function across the 10-year 125 C mission.

title: Ice cube in drink: metal phase-change buffer clamps junction peaks
idea: A sealed pocket of low-melting alloy (Sn-Bi eutectic, ~138 C) in the package lid absorbs latent heat, so at 125 C ambient, self-heating bursts are capped near the melt point instead of spiking 15-25 C higher.
why: Arrhenius: removing excursions above 125 C roughly halves worst-case leakage and aging, so the part meets 10 years at 125 C without a 145 C guard-band.

title: Quilt patches: per-row error-correcting pointers patch hot-emerging weak cells
idea: Each row carries a small on-die pointer field in a spare column (e.g. 4 pointers of address plus replacement bit); when 125 C scrubbing reveals a newly leaky cell, a pointer records it and the read path patches that bit independently of ECC.
why: Absorbs the weak population that grows over 10 years at 125 C without spending ECC strength, which stays reserved for random faults; ~1% overhead.

title: Pothole map: temperature-binned weak maps convert errors into erasures
idea: Like a road crew's pothole map, the controller keeps compact weak-cell maps per temperature bin (85/105/125 C) learned in-field; at the current temperature those positions are decoded as erasures, which cost half as much as unknown errors in RS/BCH.
why: At 125 C the weak set is large but predictable; roughly doubles effective ECC strength and allows 2-4x longer hot refresh across the 10-year life.

title: Drip irrigation: Esaki-diode trickle latch makes storage nodes self-sustaining
idea: Each storage node gets a vertical Si/SiGe interband tunnel diode to a bias line; its negative-differential-resistance curve against a matched load forms two stable voltages, so leakage is replenished continuously like drip irrigation rather than refreshed.
why: Eliminates refresh at 125 C if peak-to-valley ratio stays >~3 when hot (interband tunneling is weakly temperature dependent) and valley current stays <~10 fA/cell over 10 years.

title: Castle moat: storage node on buried insulator removes hot junction leakage
idea: The storage contact lands on a local buried-insulator island (silicon-on-nothing or lateral overgrowth), so the storage node has no p-n junction volume in the substrate and only the access channel can leak.
why: Junction SRH generation dominates the tail at 125 C; removing it cuts hot tail leakage ~5-10x, keeping standard refresh viable for 10 years.

title: Kitchen sponge: oxygen-vacancy scavenger laminate stabilizes hot capacitor leakage
idea: A 0.3-0.5 nm oxygen-reservoir layer (e.g. partially oxidized Ru/RuO2 or SrO) at the top electrode of the ZrO2/Al2O3 stack donates oxygen to refill vacancies that migrate under field at 125 C, halting the barrier lowering that raises dielectric leakage over years.
why: Hot leakage drift blocks qualifying thinner, higher-k dielectrics; stabilization lets k~40+ stacks pass 125 C/10 years, giving more charge per area (Fact 1).

title: Lizard tail autotomy: self-clearing electrodes isolate capacitor breakdown spots
idea: A lizard sheds its tail to survive: borrowing metallized-film-capacitor self-healing, the top electrode includes a 2-3 nm resistive, easily oxidized layer that clears locally around a breakdown filament, so the cell loses a sliver of area instead of shorting to the plate.
why: TDDB at 125 C for 10 years caps storage-dielectric field; benign breakdowns allow ~20% higher field (more charge or thinner dielectric).

title: Hibernating bear: hot-triggered compaction parks cold pages in strong rows
idea: Above ~105 C the controller or OS compresses cold pages 2-3x, packs them into the strongest-retention subarrays, and turns refresh off for the emptied subarrays (partial-array self-refresh).
why: Refresh power at 125 C is 4-8x room temperature; refreshing ~40% of the array cuts hot refresh energy ~60% and lowers self-heating over 10 years.

title: Rosetta stone: dual-technology copies with uncorrelated hot failure modes
idea: Critical data (page tables, ECC metadata, kernel) is written in two 'scripts': once in 1T1C DRAM and once in an oxide-channel gain-cell region whose temperature failure mechanism differs, with per-copy ECC arbitrating any mismatch.
why: At 125 C mirrored copies fail together by the same mechanism; diversity gives orders-lower silent corruption for <2% capacity, letting the bulk run thinner margins for 10 years.

title: Tea-kettle whistle: ECC error rate, not temperature, drives thermal throttling
idea: Per-bank on-die ECC correction counters feed the SoC power manager; when corrected-error rate crosses a budget, adjacent compute is throttled or cooling boosted, replacing fixed 85/95 C thresholds that assume worst-case cells.
why: Most parts survive 125 C with margin; closing the loop on the real failure signal removes conservative 2x refresh and throttling guard-bands while holding the 10-year error budget.
